questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Academic opportunities

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: I wanted to visit a University in an English speaking country first and foremost, but the ranking of the University was also of particular significance to me.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer:
I have had a wonderful stay overall and would highly recommend anyone to study abroad in Edinburgh if they are given the change.

That said, it is an expensive city (country) to live in and the heating bills were shockingly high which meant we couldn't afford having heat on during the cold periods.
In terms of the actual studies, I had hoped for more teachings since I only had 6 hours a week for 10 weeks. In Copenhagen I am used to 8 hours for 14 weeks and, considering the money other students pay to study here, I believe you'd be in your good right to expect more. The quality of the teachings though, were all fine.

questions.question: How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: Overall, I believe the information were somewhat accessible but you will need to spend some time getting to know the IT platforms of the University.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: None, but I assume I could have received assistance if needed and asked for.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
questions.answer: I think the administrative assistance is fine, but I would have hoped to be better introduced to fellow students on exchange, e.g. through a mentor programme. There were some activities arranged but unfortunately my autumn semester overlapped with the preliminary weeks of this semester which meant I had to study for my exams and miss out on most of the stuff.

questions.question: How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer: It is very difficult to find affordable housing, I believe. The postgraduate accommodation supplied by the university were oddly expensive compared to undergraduate ones. Luckily, someone suggested to me that I should look into the platform called Spare Room which is where I found my flat.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: The city is expensive when it comes to accommodation and it gets really cold inside during the winter months. So remember warm clothes and a PJ if you don't want to spend all of your SU on heating bills.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: It was difficult to find the courses that I could apply for at first, but in the end I got the ones I had wished for. You have the opportunity of swapping courses during the first few weeks of the semester which I took advantage of.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: You can place all the courses of your interest in a week calendar when you apply for the courses. That was quite helpful, I found. Still, you should be aware that the courses may take place at different locations.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: I got the three courses I had initially applied for. When I wanted to swap courses later on, I got my second priority, so all in all satisfactory.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer:
Use the online device on MyEd that places the courses in a week calendar.
Be aware that you can swap courses, so you might want to join some extra courses in the very first week. Thereby, you will be introduced to more courses and, hopefully, you'll discover the ones in your interest.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA courses at your host university? *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: I enjoyed following MA courses and found the level very similar to the one back home. I have since my arrival been told by other students from UCPH that they could only apply for BA courses due to new rules. I hope renegotiations with University of Edinburgh will enable future UCPH students to follow MA courses to fulfill the potential of the exchange.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer:
The teachings were good but in my opinion there were too few (2 hours a week for 10 weeks).

That said, I do appreciate that you get a more nuanced final grade over here: the grades you get from presentations, essays, and final essays/exams all count and constitute one final grade per course.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
The European Union in International Affairs,
Climate Change, Justice, and Responsibility
Environmental Risk: Politics, Ethics, and Communication

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
I would recommend all three but I also believe there are many other interesting courses. E.g. I would have liked to also follow the course Anthropology and Environment.

The teachers on each of my courses seemed very passionate about their research areas and, equally important, very interested in how the students felt about the topics we covered throughout the semester. 
The EU in International Affairs were very well structured; Climate Change, Justice and Responsibility provided a very interesting philosophical approach to climate change; and the course on Environmental Risks were funnily creative as we were given a lot of freedom in our essays.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: Heating bills in the winter

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer:
Most stuff were more expensive than I had expected it to be. Accommodation, food (quite similar to back home), trains etc.
Only things that I found less expensive were hair cuts and pints due to student discounts.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer:
I would have liked to play football but missed out on the trials due to my exams at UCPH. That said, it did seem quite serious and I would have preferred less competitive activities.
I believe that there a many other non-academic opportunities than sports, but sadly I did not find the time to engage with these.

questions.question: What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: I know that there are plenty sports societies but I am not too aware of the cultural and non-sport ones that surely can be found here too.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: I would recommend any future student here to start their exchange by joining a community. Again, sadly, I was distracted by my UCPH exams at that time and then had to settle in.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer:
The city itself is amazing and includes a lot of places and things worth exploring. So first of all, I encourage other students to just walk around the city and enjoy its unique architecture and green areas. 
The trains are very expensive but if you book stuff early on, you might be lucky. Otherwise, if you've got a drivers licence (I didn't) rent a car and travel the country. I went up north to Inverness and Loch Ness and drove past the West coast on my way back. I would have loved to explore a lot more of the country but being able to drive seems quite helpful around here. 
Glencoe Valley is a MUST, but Loch Ness was great too. There is also a lot of Harry Potter stuff to explore if interested - both in Edinburgh and around the country.
There are also several things nearby (St. Andrews, Glasgow, Melrose Abbey, Rosslyn Chapel, Alnwick Castle etc.).

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: The expensive student accommodation through the university turned out to do me a favour as I found a private flat instead. Here, I have been living with three English students who have introduced me to the culture, their friends, and all sorts of stuff around the city. In other words, that was surprisingly easy to me but primarily because I ended up where I did.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer:
Socialising with local students is a bit challenging if you are on exchange in the spring semester since most students seem to have settled and made a lot of friends already. That said, they seem more used to and welcoming towards exchange students than we are in Copenhagen, and they are usually impressed by our level of English (since most locals don't speak anything but English). So don't be afraid; both by flat mates, class mates, and pub mates have all been kind and welcoming towards me. It won't do any damage to join someone's table and have a drink with some strangers who might turn out to be your friends for the rest of the semester. (They might even be used to drive in the 'wrong' side of the road.)

There are many other international students who, like you, will be looking for someone to share their Scottish adventure with, so don't hesitate to reach out though it feel slightly awkward at first considering the "reserved" Danish culture.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: The culture is very similar to back home, but the Scottish Accent might be challenging at first. In Edinburgh it is less challenging though but as soon as you turn towards Glasgow or up north you'll experience a stronger accent.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer:
The pub culture is amazing! My flat mates would take me out five times to grab a beer the very first week. And I do not say that because we went out clubbing every night. To the contrary, what I found great was that we'd just go for a pint of two - nothing wild - just to catch up, and then we'd turn back home. 
Of course football is a big thing over here as well which I appreciated as it pushed me to the pubs where I met some nice people.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
Make sure to experience the city and the country while you are here. I would have loved to experience more.
Prioritise joining a society or some sort of student community in the very first weeks as they seem to do a lot of events at the start of each semester (if possible, avoid UCPH exams that overlap with the introductory weeks at UoE)
Enjoy your time here; the teachings at least are over before you know it.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer:
If you struggle finding accommodation try SpareRoom. Just like in Copenhagen, the competition is high, so write as many as possible and hopefully you'll succeed in finding a nice flat eventually.
(I lived in Newington just next to the Meadows which is a great area and close to the campus for social sciences)

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: Meeting a lot of nice people from around the world and experiencing what it is like to live in a different country.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: The cold temperatures during winter times. As stressed, do make sure to pack some warm clothes in case you don't have heating included in your monthly rent.

questions.question: Any other comments?
questions.answer: Enjoy your stay! Edinburgh is a wonderful city and the nature of Scotland really is something special! :)

questions.question: Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
